hints: Recall the definition of a transverse wave in terms of the direction of particle vibration relative to the direction of energy transfer.
teacher_walkthrough: The defining property of a transverse wave is that the particle oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of energy propagation.
Here line P is the particle vibration direction and line Q is the energy propagation direction.
Therefore for a transverse wave, $$P \perp Q$$, i.e. P is at $90^{\circ}$ to Q.
walkthrough: Mark scheme step 1: state P perpendicular to Q (or at 90 degrees).
common_pitfalls: Confusing transverse with longitudinal and stating parallel.
Describing P and Q vaguely without using perpendicular or 90 degrees.

hints: Recall the definition of a longitudinal wave in terms of the direction of particle vibration relative to the direction of energy transfer.
teacher_walkthrough: The defining property of a longitudinal wave is that the particle oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy propagation.
Here line P is the particle vibration direction and line Q is the energy propagation direction.
Therefore for a longitudinal wave, $$P \parallel Q$$, i.e. P is in the same direction as Q.
walkthrough: Mark scheme step 1: state P parallel to Q (or in same direction).
common_pitfalls: Confusing longitudinal with transverse and stating perpendicular.
Stating that the wave itself is parallel rather than comparing P and Q.

hints: Identify the wave equation linking speed, frequency and wavelength for sound.
Convert frequency from kHz to Hz before substituting $v = 340\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ and $f = 1.7\,\text{kHz}$.
teacher_walkthrough: The wave speed, frequency and wavelength are linked by $$v = f \lambda$$.
walkthrough: Mark scheme C1: use v = f lambda.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to convert 1.7 kHz to 1700 Hz, giving a wavelength 1000 times too large.
Omitting the unit m or giving wavelength in cm without conversion.

hints: Use the stationary wave pattern: antinode at the open end, node at the closed end, with antinode to antinode separation $\lambda/2$ and antinode to node separation $\lambda/4$.
teacher_walkthrough: For a tube closed at one end, there is a displacement node at the closed end and a displacement antinode at the open end.
Fig. 5.1 shows an antinode at the open end plus one more antinode inside, so from the open end inward the pattern is antinode to antinode to node at the closed end.
Antinode to antinode distance is $$\frac{\lambda}{2}$$ and antinode to node distance is $$\frac{\lambda}{4}$$.
walkthrough: Mark scheme A1: L = 3 lambda / 4 = 0.15 m.
common_pitfalls: Assuming L equals one full wavelength or lambda/2, ignoring the closed end node condition.
Miscounting antinodes and using L = 5 lambda/4 or L = lambda/4.

hints: Recall that the longest wavelength (fundamental mode) in a closed tube fits only a quarter wavelength in length L.
teacher_walkthrough: The maximum wavelength corresponds to the fundamental stationary wave with the fewest nodes and antinodes.
For a tube closed at one end the fundamental has only one antinode at the open end and one node at the closed end.
common_pitfalls: Using lambda_max = 2L, which applies to a tube open at both ends, not a tube closed at one end.
Confusing maximum wavelength with minimum frequency calculation and reusing 1.7 kHz.

hints: Apply Malus law with incident intensity $I_{0} = 8.5\,\text{W}\,\text{m}^{-2}$ and angle $\theta = 35^{\circ}$ between the incident polarisation and the transmission axis.
teacher_walkthrough: Malus law for polarised light incident on a polariser is $$I = I_{0} \cos^{2}\theta$$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the incident polarisation direction and the transmission axis.
walkthrough: Mark scheme A1: I = 8.5 cos^2 35 degrees = 5.7 W m^-2.
common_pitfalls: Using sin instead of cos, or using the angle in radians on the calculator.
Forgetting to square the cosine term and calculating 8.5 cos 35 degrees.

hints: Apply Malus law again, now with incident intensity $5.7\,\text{W}\,\text{m}^{-2}$ on the second filter and transmitted intensity $5.2\,\text{W}\,\text{m}^{-2}$.
Note the relevant angle is the difference between the two transmission axes, $\alpha - 35^{\circ}$, then solve with inverse cos and add $35^{\circ}$.
teacher_walkthrough: Malus law for the second filter is $$I_{2} = I_{1} \cos^{2}\phi$$ where $I_{1}$ is the intensity incident on it and $\phi$ is the angle between the two transmission axes.
common_pitfalls: Using alpha directly as the Malus angle instead of the difference alpha minus 35 degrees.
Using the original 8.5 W m^-2 as I1 for the second filter instead of 5.7 W m^-2.
